newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: SOCCER-S.KOREAN FOOTBALL CHIEF DISMISSES FIFA ATTACK.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-S.KOREAN FOOTBALL CHIEF DISMISSES FIFA ATTACK.

text.p: South Korea's soccer chief on Thursday hit out at reported criticism by FIFA general secretary Sepp Blatter that bickering between Korea and Japan was hampering the build-up to the 2002 World Cup finals.
Chung Mong-joon also repeated his suggestion Japan and South Korea should stage a play-off to decide which country hosts the final match.
"I think it would be an exciting way of deciding the matter," he said in a written answer to questions submitted by Reuters.

The Asian neighbours with a history of mutual loathing were jointly awarded the finals in May after a bidding contest so bitter and costly that FIFA could not bring itself to choose an outright winner.
"I think it is very strange that anyone should be suggesting that there have been difficulties in getting us to co-operate," Chung said.
"Nobody can stop co-hosting or prevent a magnificent first World Cup for Asia."
Chung, a leading business tycoon and a member of parliament, is president of the South Korea soccer federation and led the country's bid for the finals.
Blatter was quoted as saying in an interview in November's World Soccer magazine that, far from coming closer, South Korea and Japan were moving further apart.
"This is not the marriage we want," he reportedly said.
Blatter said it was hard enough simply to arrange a date for representatives of the countries to meet, and he complained they were at odds over how many teams should compete.
Japan wanted to invite 40 teams so matches could be spread out among more cities, while South Korea was insisting on 32, Blatter said.

Chung said Japan and South Korea had made no progress on the organisation of the finals because FIFA, in a letter from Blatter, had specifically instructed them to hold off until a FIFA working group had made its report.
As for the reported dispute over teams, Chung said: "I cannot understand why anyone would be suggesting there is a dispute between Korea and Japan, because Korea has not commented on this matter."
He added that Blatter's comments were "not in anybody's interests".
Chung said a play-off was just one way of resolving the thorniest question of the World Cup finals -- which country will get the honour of the last match.
"But there are other options," he said.

Chung has previously suggested, only slightly tongue-in-cheek, that since Japan had boasted so loudly about its virtual-reality technology, the final should be played in South Korea and beamed to Japan where fans could watch the match as though it was live in front of them.

"There are many issues to be resolved for the successful co-hosting but with the honesty and commitment of all parties involved, I know we can reach agreement to stage a fantastic World Cup," Chung said.
